 singapore New SGH Emergency-NNI building opens, designed around patients' journeys
 The 12-storey building centralises assessment, treatment and recovery in one connected space. The new Singapore General Hospital Emergency/NNI Building. PHOTO: AsiaOne/Ong Chin Wee PUBLISHED ON October 30, 2026 9:01 AM BY Sean Ler The Republic's oldest hospital, Singapore General Hospital (SGH), officially opened its new SGH Emergency/National Neuroscience Institute (NNI) building on Friday (Oct 31).
 Established in 1821, Singapore's first general hospital started out in a wooden shed near Bras Basah and Stamford Roads. Amongst the older generation, it is commonly referred to as "See Pai Poh" because of its 1882 relocation to Sepoy Lines along Outram Road. 
 Fast forward to 1948, SGH established its Casualty and Outpatient Service that is today known as the Emergency Department, and the NNI later in 1999. 
 Explaining why the two medical disciplines are housed together at the building's opening ceremony, Minister for Health Ong Ye Kung pointed out at the official opening on Friday that emergency department patients today are older and many have multiple chronic conditions.
 "Emergency care requires thoughtful clinical judgement and careful assessment, with several specialties working together," he said.
 SGH and NNI said in a joint news release after the opening that the vision behind the 12-storey building is a model of emergency care built entirely around the patient journey, where assessment, diagnosis, intervention, and recovery happen in one seamlessly connected space. 
 Singapore's first ED angiography suite
 Head of SGH's Department of Emergency Medicine Dr Ivan Chua, elaborating on the journey, explained: "Patients can move easily from emergency assessment to acute medical care, neuroscience intervention, or advanced imaging as their condition requires."
 He added that this allows different teams to collaborate more effectively, bringing expertise from multiple disciplines to provide coordinated responses for complex medical conditions.
 According to the healthcare institution, in cases such as a stroke — where time is of the essence — a patient can be assessed, scanned, and treated for an acute stroke without leaving the building in as quickly as 82 minutes.
 The new building also houses Singapore's first emergency department-based angiography suite, further enhancing stroke care, and enabling patients to undergo endovascular thrombectomy (EVT), a life-saving intervention to reopen blocked blood vessels in the brain within minutes of diagnosis, without being transferred to other blocks.
 [[nid:724390]]
 Over 150 short-stay beds
 And beyond the 53 critical care area cubicles and 12 resuscitation rooms, the building also houses acute medical wards with over 150 short-stay beds, neuroscience specialist outpatient clinics, and advanced imaging, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and interventional radiology.
 Meanwhile, patient comfort and experience have also been factored into the new building's design, with private treatment areas featuring walls and sliding doors that offer dignity in what can be a vulnerable moment during medical emergencies.
 Then, there are also projector technology that casts calming visuals during MRI scans, to reduce anxiety in an environment that many find distressing.
 While waiting, families can also receive real-time information through patient information systems, lessening uncertainty during an already difficult time.
 Panic button for healthcare workers
 Healthcare workers are also "looked after", with a Code Grey panic button system implemented in the new premises. 
 During its trial at the former emergency department, this was found to have led to a four-time reduction in response time for assistance when a staff member encounters abusive behaviours at work.
 Deputy head of ambulatory services (Neuroscience clinic@SGH) Dr Tushar Divakar Gosavi said that the multi-disciplinary clinics in the new building allow neurologists to easily discuss and refer patients for assessment by therapists, with more urgent cases being seen the same time, where appointment slots permit.
 Short intravenous infusions for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease and migraine can now be administered at the clinic’s new infusion room, and lumbar punctures can also be performed onsite.
 "This avoids the need for patients to be warded overnight, thereby freeing up beds for patients waiting in the Emergency Department to be admitted," the hospital said.
 The official opening of the building marks another milestone in the 20-year SGH Campus Masterplan, following the earlier completion of SingHealth Tower and Outram Community Hospital in 2019, and the National Cancer Centre in 2023.
 In the years ahead, the Elective Care Centre, the new National Dental Centre, and the Health Sciences Authority and Ministry of Health buildings will also be progressively completed.
 Said the health minister: "We will continue to invest in our healthcare infrastructure and our people, so that we can all look forward to a rejuvenated health campus, and a stronger healthcare system that can provide even better care to Singaporeans."
